subtopics.title: Congestion Window and Loss Signals
subtopics.summary: How classic TCP infers congestion end-to-end since IP gives no explicit feedback: the congestion window (cwnd) limits the sending rate, arriving ACKs signal a congestion-free path and permit increases, while loss events (triple duplicate ACKs vs. timeouts) signal congestion and trigger decreases.

subtopics.title: Slow Start
subtopics.summary: The initial slow-start phase: cwnd starts small and grows exponentially (doubling per RTT) as ACKs arrive, until the slow-start threshold (ssthresh) or a loss event ends the phase; also its contribution to connection latency.

subtopics.title: Congestion Avoidance and AIMD
subtopics.summary: The steady-state additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease (AIMD) behavior: cwnd grows linearly by 1 MSS per RTT and is halved on a triple duplicate-ACK loss, producing the saw-tooth pattern as TCP probes for the available bandwidth.

subtopics.title: Fast Recovery
subtopics.summary: Reacting to loss without a timeout: fast retransmit of the missing segment after three duplicate ACKs, halving cwnd and continuing transmission (Reno-style fast recovery), contrasted with the timeout-driven reset to slow start (Tahoe).

subtopics.title: AIMD Fairness
subtopics.summary: Why AIMD yields an equal share of a congested link's bandwidth among competing TCP connections: the additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease dynamics converge competing flows toward equal throughput.
